item.title: Elon Musk defrauded Twitter investors in $44B buyout, jury finds
item.description: Technology billionaire and Tesla CEO Elon Musk committed securities fraud with false or misleading statements about Twitter’s fake bot accounts as he attempted to scrap or renegotiate the $44 billion deal to buy the social media platform, a California jury for a civil trial unanimously found Friday.

item.title: 2 lawyers convicted in staged truck accidents scheme
item.description: Two personal injury lawyers have been convicted by a federal jury in New Orleans for participating in a scheme to stage collisions with tractor-trailer trucks to collect large settlement payouts.

item.title: Goldman Sachs
item.description: The top lawyer at the Goldman Sachs Group Inc., who has been linked to disgraced multimillionaire financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, secured a $25 million pay package and new security perks in 2025 before she announced her upcoming resignation in June.

item.title: Google
item.description: Relatives of a Florida man who died by suicide after planning an act of “mass casualty” at the Miami International Airport are suing Google, alleging that its Gemini artificial intelligence chatbot escalated persuasive dialogue that caused the tragedy.

item.title: Musicians in this state are suing AI companies under biometric privacy law
item.description: Musicians who argue that artificial intelligence companies have used their songs without permission are bringing litigation under a unique law in Illinois.

item.title: Legalweek 2026: Home bases, agentic AI and the race to own the lawyer’s desktop
item.description: Change is never easy, whether it’s transitioning your firm to generative artificial intelligence tools or acclimating to a new location for one of your favorite legal technology conferences. I was faced with the latter challenge earlier this month, when Legalweek, long hosted at the Midtown Hilton in New York City, moved to the Jacob K. Javits Convention Center on the western edge of Manhattan.

item.title: Highlights from the Legalweek
item.description: Ari Kaplan, a legal industry analyst and the host of the Reinventing Professionals podcast, recently spoke with attendees at the 2026 Legalweek conference about current trends and opportunities in the legal sector for his annual mixtape.

item.title: Job satisfaction gap found between equity partners, others at their firms, new survey says
item.description: Nonequity partners and associates at law firms are less satisfied with their jobs than equity partners, a new Bloomberg Law survey has found.

item.title: Attorney at social media addiction trial takes selfie, receives $1,100 sanction
item.description: A plaintiffs lawyer recently received a $1,100 sanction for taking a selfie and conducting a Zoom interview from inside the Los Angeles Superior Court during the first trial alleging that Meta Platforms and YouTube caused addictions in adolescents.

item.title: Baseline Drafting: What skills are some lawyers missing?
item.description: Law schools are sometimes faulted for not “teaching students to write well,” as if the goal were to mint stylists on demand. That’s not the complaint here. Let’s focus instead on a narrower problem: the concern that many graduates never learn even a small set of baseline drafting and advocacy ideas that every practicing lawyer should know. These are points so basic that they ought to be treated as shared professional grammar, not as optional refinements for aficionados.

item.title: Drug convictions bar lawyer from bench but not from practicing law
item.description: A criminal defense attorney whose felony drug convictions prevented him from becoming a judge can still practice law, according to a March 17 order from the Montana Supreme Court.

item.title: Lawyer gets prison time for defrauding clients of over $700K
item.description: A West Virginia attorney who defrauded clients of more than $700,000 has been sentenced to 97 months in federal prison, federal prosecutors said.

item.title: Firms hire fewer Black law interns because of conservative pressure
item.description: The number of Black summer associates at U.S. law firms has decreased to its lowest level in more than a decade amid a conservative push to end race- and gender-based preferences in school admissions and hiring, including a specific effort against legal internships, according to a story by Bloomberg Law.

item.title: 1 in 3 GCs who left Fortune 500 companies were in role less than 3 years, new report says
item.description: More than half of general counsels hired in 2025 were external candidates, marking a shift from the previous year when the majority were internal hires, according to a new report from executive search company Russell Reynolds Associates.
